source: Wang, Mao, Fried, Neubig (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: An LLM extracts common sub-routines from several successful trajectories, abstracts away example-specific values, and stores them as workflows. This is the closest working LLM version of merging overlapping episodes into shared structure.
numbers: WebArena (812 tasks, gpt-4-0613, temp 0): total success 35.5% vs BrowserGym baseline 23.5% (+12.0 points, +51.1% relative); about 2.0 fewer steps per task. Beat SteP (33.0%, 14 human-written workflows). Most of the gain appears within about 40 examples.
quote: prompt the agent to extract common sub-routines from one or more input experiences
limits: Workflows are induced per website group, and only from episodes a judge calls correct. Online induction can store wrong workflows. Main table uses one model family (gpt-4).
agent_relevance: Direct template for a subgoal library: induce from several overlapping solved cases, not one, and replace specifics with slots.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory, ablations and generalization
finding: Abstract sub-routines beat storing whole concrete examples. Rule-based and LLM-based induction perform about the same. Online induction (from test queries) generalizes better as the train-test gap grows.
numbers: Mind2Web vs Synapse (retrieves whole examples): +5.0 element accuracy, +4.0 step success. WebArena rule vs LM induction: 0.1 point success gap, LM 0.4 fewer steps. Mind2Web cross-domain, gpt-4: step SR 35.5 (online) vs 32.6 (offline) vs 18.6 (MindAct); full-task SR only 1.7 / 0.7 / 1.0.
limits: Full-task success on Mind2Web stays at 1 to 5 percent, so the gains are at step level. Workflows built on earlier workflows ('find place' then 'get zip code') are shown by case study, not by a controlled test.
agent_relevance: Store the abstract routine with specifics as parameters. A simple rule-based merge may be nearly as good as an LLM merge, so test the cheap one first.

source: Ouyang et al. (2025) ReasoningBank: Scaling Agent Self-Evolving with Reasoning Memory
finding: Extracts strategy items from both successes and failures using a judge, stores them, and scales test-time compute so parallel attempts give contrastive signal. Consolidation itself is only 'simple addition', no merging. It beats AWM and Synapse.
numbers: WebArena overall SR, no memory / Synapse / AWM / ReasoningBank / +MaTTS (n=684): Gemini-2.5-flash 40.5 / 42.1 / 44.1 / 48.8 / 51.8; Gemini-2.5-pro 46.7 / 47.7 / 47.6 / 53.9 / 56.3; Claude-3.7-sonnet 41.7 / 42.6 / 40.8 / 46.3 / 48.8. Up to 16% fewer steps.
quote: successful experiences contribute validated strategies, while failed ones supply counterfactual signals
limits: AWM was below no-memory for Claude-3.7-sonnet (40.8 vs 41.7) and gained only 0.9 for Gemini-2.5-pro. So a success-only merge can be neutral or harmful depending on the model. Judge labels are noisy. Authors kept consolidation deliberately simple.
agent_relevance: Lessons from failures add what success-only merging lacks. A published merge method can fail to transfer across models, so measure per model.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Agentic Context Engineering (ACE)
finding: Grow-and-refine: append new bullet items, update existing ones in place, then de-duplicate by embedding similarity. It avoids letting the LLM rewrite the whole context, which causes context collapse.
numbers: Average +10.6% on agent tasks (AppWorld) and +8.6% on finance tasks over strong baselines. AppWorld, DeepSeek-V3.1: ReAct+ACE 59.4 vs 42.4 base (+17.0) on one split. Adaptation latency down 82.3% and rollouts down 75.1% vs GEPA (AppWorld offline).
limits: Gains depend on a good reflector and on execution feedback. Authors say performance falls below base only under sustained adversarial corruption. Not a pure test of merging, because several parts change together.
agent_relevance: Merge by incremental edits plus a dedup pass, never by free rewrite of the whole library. Fits the schema style: code does bookkeeping, model fills slots.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) ACE: context collapse case and dedup threshold ablation
finding: Full LLM rewriting of an accumulated context destroyed information in one step. Changing how aggressively near-duplicates are merged gave non-monotone results.
numbers: Collapse: context 18,282 tokens and accuracy 66.7 at step 60; next step 122 tokens and accuracy 57.1, below the no-adaptation baseline 63.7. Dedup threshold on FiNER (DeepSeek-V3.1, base 70.7): 50% gives 77.0, 70% gives 73.9, 90% gives 78.6.
limits: One task and one model for the threshold ablation. Differences of a few points, no variance reported.
agent_relevance: Merging is a risk as well as a gain. Keep raw items recoverable and log every merge. Best strictness is not predictable, so treat it as a tunable.

source: Suzgun, Yuksekgonul, Bianchi, Jurafsky, Zou (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet
finding: A persistent, self-curated memory of strategies and code snippets, rewritten by the model after each query (DC-Cu), or retrieved and synthesized per query (DC-RS). Compact curated memory beats appending full history.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet +27 points on AIME 2024 and +30 on AIME 2025 under DC-Cu; GPT-4o Game of 24 from about 10% to 99% (reused Python solution); Math Equation Balancer 45-50% to 98-100%; GPQA-Diamond +9; MMLU-Pro Eng/Physics +8.
limits: Authors report it is not a panacea: smaller models (GPT-4o-mini, Claude 3.5 Haiku) gain little because they produce too few correct solutions and cannot refine stored content. Gains are largest where one reusable trick (code) exists.
agent_relevance: A merged library is only as good as the solutions merged. Do not consolidate a weak solver's output without a check (G2, G3).

source: Xu et al. (2025) A-MEM: Agentic Memory for LLM Agents
finding: Zettelkasten-style notes. Link generation connects a new note to similar old notes. Memory evolution lets old notes be rewritten when a related new one arrives.
numbers: LoCoMo ablation, GPT-4o-mini, F1: multi-hop 9.65 without both modules, 21.35 without evolution, 27.02 full; temporal 24.55 / 31.24 / 45.85; adversarial 15.32 / 44.16 / 50.03 (reading of a messy table). About 1,200 tokens per memory operation; 85-93% fewer tokens than LoCoMo/MemGPT baselines.
limits: Baselines were sometimes better on open-domain and adversarial categories. Conversation QA, not reasoning. Table extraction was messy: check the paper before quoting single cells.
agent_relevance: Linking before editing carries most of the gain. For our library: find the overlap set first, then edit, and keep the old version.

source: Fang et al. (2025) LightMem: Lightweight and Efficient Memory-Augmented Generation
finding: Explicitly sleep-inspired. At test time entries are only appended (soft update). In offline 'sleep' it builds, per entry, a queue of similar older entries (later entries may update earlier ones only), then de-duplicates, abstracts and resolves conflicts in parallel.
numbers: LongMemEval and LoCoMo: QA accuracy up to +7.7% / +29.3%; total tokens down up to 38x / 20.9x; API calls down up to 30x / 55.5x; online-only cost down up to 106x / 117x tokens. LoCoMo GPT-4o-mini about 72-73% best settings vs 71.83 FullText and 64.16 A-MEM (from a messy table).
quote: LLMs can be unreliable when tasked with complex real-time update operations
limits: Authors' own comparison on two conversation-memory benchmarks. The extracted tables do not clearly isolate how much the offline step alone adds.
agent_relevance: Closest published LLM analogue to overlap-based consolidation: decouple storing from merging, merge offline, compare only similar items. Matches a sleep step between tasks.

source: Fang et al. (2025) LightMem, soft versus hard update case
finding: Argues that real-time merging by an LLM can wrongly treat two related but compatible facts as a conflict and delete the older one. Append first, merge later.
numbers: Worked example only: 'planning a trip to Tokyo' (Monday 2 PM) plus 'trains to Kyoto' (4 PM). Hard update gives 'User plans Kyoto trip' and loses Tokyo; soft update keeps both. No measured error rate.
limits: Illustrative case, not a measured error rate.
agent_relevance: Never merge on the fly. Keep unmerged items and merge only in an offline pass with a check (supports G2).

source: Bowers et al. (2023) Top-Down Synthesis for Library Learning (Stitch)
finding: Finds abstractions that compress shared structure across a corpus of programs, using top-down search and pruning. A fast, exact, symbolic answer to 'what do these overlapping solutions share'.
numbers: 3-4 orders of magnitude faster and 2 orders less memory than DreamCoder's compression. Eight graphics domains: test-set compression ratio 2.55x to 11.57x, 0.19 s to 60.16 s, 11.21 MB to 714.55 MB peak memory.
limits: Needs programs in a DSL, so it fits code-like rules, not free text.
agent_relevance: If subgoal rules are written as code or structured rules, use a symbolic compressor to find shared parts instead of asking the model. Cheap and checkable.

source: Ellis et al. (2020) DreamCoder: wake-sleep Bayesian program learning
finding: Wake: solve tasks. Abstraction sleep: refactor solved programs into shared library routines. Dreaming sleep: train the search network on replayed and imagined problems. A literal computational model of replay-based abstraction.
numbers: Text editing: trained on 128 tasks, tested on 108 SyGuS problems. Before learning 3.7% solved in 10 min (mean 235 s); after 79.6% (mean 40 s). CVC4 82.4% (1 h, 8 CPUs); DreamCoder 84.3% with that generous budget. About 20 new routines in list processing; rediscovered filter.
limits: Ablations (no abstraction, no dreaming) are in a figure; exact values not captured here. Original compression search was slow (fixed later by Stitch).
agent_relevance: The abstraction phase has the best evidence for helping later search. Use it as the design model for the subgoal library.

source: Grand, Wong et al. (2024) LILO: Learning Interpretable Libraries by Compressing and Documenting Code
finding: LLM writes programs, Stitch compresses them into abstractions, an LLM auto-documents each abstraction with a name and docstring. Without the documentation step the LLM used compressed abstractions poorly.
numbers: Online synthesis, mean test solve rate, LILO vs DreamCoder: REGEX 77.07 vs 43.93 (+33.14), LOGO +20.42, CLEVR +2.26 (DreamCoder already 94.50). LILO vs LLM-solver-only: +0.94, +8.09, +16.82. Max train REGEX: LILO 93.20 vs 63.80 for search-only variant; 3 seeds.
quote: naively providing a LLM with Stitch abstractions measurably degraded its ability to
limits: Three synthetic domains. LLM prior knowledge alone beats DreamCoder on REGEX by +32.20, so part of the gain is not from the library. Offline results were mixed across variants.
agent_relevance: Merged rules must be named and described in plain words, or the model will not use them. Add a naming step to every merge.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager
finding: Skill library of verified executable skills indexed by description; new skills compose old ones. No merging or de-duplication. The library helps late in the tech tree.
numbers: 3.3x more unique items, 2.3x longer distance, tech milestones up to 15.3x faster than prior best. Tech tree, 3 runs, mean prompting iterations with vs without library: wooden 6 vs 7; stone 11 vs 9; iron 21 vs 29; diamond 102 (1 of 3 runs) vs not reached.
limits: Three runs each. The library did not help the early levels (stone was slower with it). It only adds, so overlap is never merged.
agent_relevance: Skill reuse pays off on deep tasks, not shallow ones. Expect little gain from a library on easy problems.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion
finding: Verbal reflections on failed attempts are stored in episodic memory and reused. A single-episode lesson, not a merge of overlapping episodes. The no-merge control.
numbers: ALFWorld: 130 of 134 tasks solved with ReAct+Reflexion (+22% absolute over baseline in 12 steps); HotPotQA +20%; HumanEval 91% pass@1.
limits: Reflections are per task. No cross-task generalization claimed.
agent_relevance: Single-episode lessons work. The open question is whether merging many of them adds more, which AWM and ExpeL test.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners
finding: Insights are extracted by comparing success-failure pairs and from lists of successes. Operators ADD, EDIT, UPVOTE, DOWNVOTE edit a shared insight list; an insight whose count reaches zero is removed. A vote-based merge across overlapping experiences.
numbers: Insights-only vs retrieval-only: HotpotQA 36% vs 31%; ALFWorld 50% vs 55%; WebShop 37% vs 38% (score 0.675 vs 0.67). ExpeL matches Reflexion on HotpotQA (40% at round 3 vs 39%).
limits: Adding reflections into insight extraction hurt performance in the ablation. Insights from gpt-4 beat those from gpt-3.5. Hand-written insights helped less than LLM ones.
agent_relevance: Insights help reasoning tasks; concrete trajectories help action tasks. A vote count with removal at zero is a cheap merge rule with a guard against bad lessons.

source: Park et al. (2023) Generative Agents
finding: A reflection step synthesizes recent memories into higher-level statements, triggered when summed importance of recent events passes 150. Reflection trees are recursive, so conclusions can cite earlier conclusions.
numbers: Believability (TrueSkill, 100 raters): full architecture best; no reflection mu=26.88; no reflection or planning 25.64; crowdworker humans 22.95; no memory, planning or reflection 21.21. Full vs prior-work baseline d = 8.16.
limits: Interview believability, not task accuracy. Ablated agents do not follow the same path as the full one.
agent_relevance: Reflection is a merge of many observations into a gist. A counted trigger (importance sum) fits G1: consolidate on a signal, not on a whim.

source: Gutierrez et al. (2024) HippoRAG
finding: Builds a knowledge graph of entities from passages (pattern separation) and retrieves by spreading activation from query entities (pattern completion). Overlapping passages are linked through shared entities.
numbers: Single-step retrieval: up to +20 points R@5 and +11 R@2 on 2WikiMultiHopQA, about +3 on MuSiQue, competitive but not best on HotpotQA. With IRCoT, further gains up to 4% (MuSiQue) and 20% (2Wiki).
limits: Weaker on HotpotQA, which needs less knowledge integration. Gains concentrate on entity-centric data. This is retrieval, not abstraction.
agent_relevance: Shared entities are a cheap way to find which stored items overlap. Use as the overlap finder before merging.

source: Zheng et al. (2025) SkillWeaver
finding: Agent explores a site, turns practice into API-like skills, tests and debugs them, and grows a library. Skills from a strong agent transfer to weaker ones.
numbers: WebArena success 25% to 38% after 160 iterations (+31.8% relative); Online-Mind2Web +39.8% relative; transfer to weaker agents up to +54.3% on WebArena.
limits: Authors note models are not robust at calling APIs. Library grows by addition; no test of merging near-duplicates.
agent_relevance: A tested skill is worth more than a merged one. Run the check (G3) before an item enters the library.

source: Cai et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Tool Makers (LATM)
finding: A strong model makes a reusable tool from a few instances; a cheaper model uses it. The once-off cost of making the tool is spread over many uses. Abstract and intro read; cost figures not recorded.
numbers: With GPT-4 as maker and GPT-3.5 as user, performance is reported as comparable to GPT-4 alone at lower average cost (exact numbers not recorded here).
limits: Tool made from a few demonstrations, not from merging many overlapping cases.
agent_relevance: Splitting 'make the rule' (rare, strong, checked) from 'use the rule' (frequent, cheap) matches a sleep/wake split.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Sleep-time Compute
finding: The model 'thinks' offline about a stored context before any question arrives, then answers from the pre-computed notes. Same shape as offline replay.
numbers: About 5x less test-time compute for equal accuracy on Stateful GSM-Symbolic and Stateful AIME; scaling sleep-time compute adds up to +13% (GSM) and +18% (AIME) accuracy; Multi-Query GSM-Symbolic: average cost per query 2.5x lower when shared across related queries.
limits: Works when questions are predictable from the context; the paper finds predictability correlates with benefit. Not tested on merging across tasks.
agent_relevance: Offline passes pay off when later queries overlap with each other, the same condition gist extraction needs.

source: Fountas et al. (2025) EM-LLM: human-inspired episodic memory for infinite context
finding: Splits token streams into events at Bayesian surprise, refines boundaries with graph methods, retrieves by similarity plus temporal contiguity. Event segmentation, a sibling of consolidation.
numbers: Evaluated on LongBench and InfiniteBench with LLaMA-3.1-8B; reported to beat RAG and full-context on part of LongBench (per-task numbers not recorded here).
limits: Segmentation and retrieval, not merging across events. Only abstract and intro read.
agent_relevance: Boundary choice shapes what can later be merged; surprise-based splitting is a cheap code-side signal.

source: Zhong et al. (2023) MemoryBank
finding: Stores event summaries and a personality summary, and lets memories decay or strengthen by a forgetting-curve rule.
numbers: Evaluated qualitatively and with small human ratings on a companion chatbot; no benchmark numbers recorded.
limits: Weak evaluation. Summaries are per day, not merged across overlapping events.
agent_relevance: Decay by use gives a prune rule for the library; evidence is thin, so treat it as a design option.

source: Memory in the Age of AI Agents: A Survey (2026)
finding: Section 5.2.1 sorts consolidation into local merging of near-duplicates, cluster-level fusion and global integration. Names RMM (LLM decides whether to merge top-K similar items, to limit wrong generalization) and CAM (clusters overlapping semantic graphs into hierarchical schemata).
numbers: No pooled effect size. Taxonomy covers LightMem, G-Memory, Mem0, Zep, MemGPT and others.
quote: A central challenge is determining the granularity at which new memories should be matched and merged
limits: A survey; cited systems are not compared on one benchmark. It calls matching granularity a central open problem.
agent_relevance: Start with local merging (lowest risk) and an explicit merge-or-not decision step.

source: Sorrenti et al. (2023) Wake-Sleep Consolidated Learning
finding: Neural continual learning with wake, NREM (replay from short- and long-term memory) and REM (dreamed new images) stages.
numbers: Tiny-ImageNet1/2, ER-ACE, final accuracy / forward transfer: wake only 4.70 / -0.93; wake+REM 25.68 / 11.89; wake+NREM 27.61 / -0.67; all three 35.68 / 8.60. Benefit kept with 30% noise in dreams.
limits: Image classification, not language. Authors' own method and benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Replay (NREM) stabilises old knowledge while a separate generative step helps transfer. A language analogue is untested.

source: van de Ven, Siegelmann, Tolias (2020) Brain-inspired replay for continual learning
finding: Only generative replay methods keep good class-incremental performance; feedback-connection replay (RtF) roughly halves the cost.
numbers: Split MNIST class-IL: fine-tune lower bound 19.90, EWC 19.90, SI 20.04, LwF 24.17, DGR 91.24, DGR+distill 91.84, RtF 92.56, offline upper bound 97.93. Permuted MNIST class-IL: DGR+distill 96.38, RtF 96.23, EWC 25.04.
limits: Small image benchmarks. Replayed samples are single items, not merged gist.
agent_relevance: Replay beats regularisation when classes must be told apart: evidence for replaying cases rather than only keeping rules.

source: Lewis and Durrant (2011) Overlapping memory replay during sleep builds cognitive schemata
finding: Source theory: replay of overlapping memories repeats shared elements most, so shared structure is strengthened and unshared detail fades. Not opened this session; named from background knowledge, no numbers claimed.
numbers: not read
limits: Theory paper. Human findings belong to the angle A and B files of this subfield.
agent_relevance: The model our merge step copies: replay overlapping items together and keep what repeats.

source: Tadros, Krishnan, Ramyaa, Bazhenov (2022) Sleep-like unsupervised replay reduces catastrophic forgetting
finding: Spiking-network model where offline noise-driven replay restores old tasks and builds joint representations of overlapping features. Not opened this session; recalled, no numbers claimed.
numbers: not read
limits: Not verified here.
agent_relevance: Computational support for overlap-driven consolidation without stored data.

source: McClelland, McNaughton, O'Reilly (1995) Complementary learning systems
finding: Foundational argument for interleaved replay from a fast store into a slow store so new items do not overwrite shared structure. Not opened this session; no numbers claimed.
numbers: not read
limits: Not verified here.
agent_relevance: Reason for offline interleaved merging: avoid overwriting by the latest case.

source: Gap note for angle C: no direct LLM test of overlap-weighted replay
finding: Across the opened papers, none compares merging overlapping items against merging non-overlapping items, or tests replay order. LLM systems append, vote, or cluster. The human claim (overlap drives gist) is untested in LLM agents.
numbers: 0 direct tests in 22 opened papers. WebSearch quota was used up; arXiv API, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate-limited, so coverage came from known arXiv ids.
limits: Absence of evidence from a limited search. Possibly missed: LLM false-memory (DRM) studies, in-context schema induction studies.
agent_relevance: Run our own test: merge overlap sets vs merge random sets vs no merge, same solver, held-out tasks.
